newsitem.title: USA: U.S. zinc premiums soften, aluminum spot quiet.
newsitem.headline: U.S. zinc premiums soften, aluminum spot quiet.

text.p: U.S. zinc spot premiums have softened a touch further despite LME prices soaring to four and 3/4 year highs and offtake under long term contract still buoyant, dealers said.

"I think part of the problem in the summer months is that anyone holding inventory gets a little nervous and wants to find a home for it," a producer-backed agent said. "A thin spot market in summer is a recipe for premiums to weaken."
Dealer quoted spot premiums at 4.50 to 4.75 cents a lb over LME cash. A few dealers said there was even talk of premiums as low as 4.25 cents.
Spot business was fairly quiet. "A lot of people are closing the first two weeks of July so they are covered," a merchant said.
The U.S. Stockpile sold a further 1,735 tonnes of metal on Wednesday, half going to one buyer, Trademet.
Three months LME zinc finished the London midday kerb at $1,383 a tonne. "I think zinc seems to be looking at $1,400 short-term and $1,475 longer term," a bullish dealer said.

Aluminum premiums have also lost some of their earlier robustness as dealings quietened down and the trading range lowered to 4.50 to 5.00 cents a lb over LME cash on nearby spot deliveries. Third quarter premiums were at 4.50 cents, with 4.00 to 4.25 cents in the fourth quarter.
"There is not much interest in spot," a merchant said.
Christopher Hill of Gerald Metals said the physical market was steadily active, but not robust as consumers were being more savvy with their buying.
"With the summer coming upon us, we are seeing signs of a little bit of cooling off in the need for metal," Hill said. "But the market continues to remain reasonably healthy."
Nickel premiums remain in the 9 to 11 cents per lb range over LME cash for melting grade metal.
"I think the nickel market is a non-event right now," a producer sales agent said. "There is plenty of scrap and nickel around. Inco has to be out for a long time to affect overall nickel prices."

Inco Ltd spokesman David Allen said Thursday that talks between the union leaders representing workers out on strike since June 2, and the company will start at 1400 EDT. A deal was expected during the weekend, he added.
"The market is not reacting at all to Inco. However, it's not going down which, in the view of some, is indicative of strength," a dealer said. "Levels of business are very good."
Tin was quiet with premiums barely changed, traders said.
